_meta.source: Port pin is the Port Autonome d'Abidjan node from OpenStreetMap (5.3043, -4.0231); the cruise berth itself is the grain terminal on the north side of the basin, addressed by OSM to Quai Nord. Every POI below was resolved individually against OpenStreetMap via Nominatim on 2026-07-30 — none is estimated. Grand-Bassam is 39 km east and is included because it is the excursion the page recommends; Yamoussoukro is 239 km away, is not feasible on a port day, and is deliberately off this map.

port_pin.label: Port Autonome d'Abidjan — the cruise berth

bbox_hint.note: Abidjan is built around a lagoon system. The port and the berth are in Treichville on the south side; Plateau, the high-rise district, faces it across the water; Cocody is north-east; Banco National Park is north-west inside the city boundary; and Grand-Bassam is 39 km east along the coast.

pois.name: Port Autonome d'Abidjan — cruise berth
pois.notes: Alongside at the grain terminal on the north side of the basin, in Treichville. There is no cruise terminal — the port authority lists nine and none is for passengers. Regulation prohibits public access inside the customs enclosure and requires a pass from the Port Commander for any person or vehicle.

pois.name: Vridi
pois.notes: The canal cut through the sandbar in 1950, giving the lagoon a deep-water entrance and creating the modern city. 300 m wide, 18 m deep, no lock, no overhead obstruction; the limit is 15.5 m draft with no length restriction.

pois.name: Treichville
pois.notes: The commune the port sits in, named for Marcel Treich-Laplène. Lively, dense, and unusual in that its streets are numbered 1 to 47 rather than named. Took significant casualties in the 2010-11 crisis.

pois.name: Marché de Treichville
pois.notes: The big covered market — wax prints, textiles, spices, music. Also precisely the crowded-market environment the US State Department flags for petty crime. Go with a guide and carry almost nothing.

pois.name: Le Plateau
pois.notes: The high-rise business district across the lagoon, about 4 km from the berth. Holds the parliament, Constitutional Council and Supreme Court — Abidjan keeps the machinery of government even though Yamoussoukro is the political capital. Compact and walkable in daylight; note the prohibition on photographing government buildings.

pois.name: Cathédrale Saint-Paul
pois.notes: Aldo Spirito's concrete cross, anchored to the nave by seven steel cables so the building appears to lean toward the lagoon. Foundation stone laid by John Paul II on 11 May 1980, dedicated by him 10 August 1985, built for about US$12 million. 370 m² of stained glass inside, including the arrival of missionaries in Côte d'Ivoire.

pois.name: La Pyramide
pois.notes: Rinaldo Olivieri's 1968-73 brutalist tower, intended 'to capture the activity of an African market in an urban setting' — housing above, retail below. Now derelict. A drive-past landmark rather than a visit.

pois.name: Musée des Civilisations de Côte d'Ivoire
pois.notes: The national ethnographic collection — masks, bronzes, regalia. Worth an hour if the excursion includes it, but confirm it is open: current hours could not be established from a primary source.

pois.name: Cocody
pois.notes: The embassy, university and villa quarter north-east of Plateau, about 8 km from the berth.

pois.name: Hôtel Ivoire
pois.notes: Opened 7 September 1963; the 100 m, 24-storey tower added 1969. Site of clashes with French UN forces in 2004 in which two demonstrators were killed. Reopened 15 May 2015 as the Sofitel. The ice rink, opened 1970 and the first in West Africa, closed decades ago and is now a banquet hall — a very commonly repeated stale fact.

pois.name: Parc National du Banco
pois.notes: Genuine rainforest inside the city boundary, with buttress-rooted trees and the well-known open-air fanico laundry where washermen work the river stones.

pois.name: Grand-Bassam
pois.notes: 39 km east — 35 min free-flow, realistically 60-90. The first French colonial capital from 1893, abandoned in 1900 after the 1899 yellow fever epidemic, UNESCO-inscribed in 2012. The Quartier France survives as a grid of colonial buildings between the lagoon and the sea. The standard cruise excursion, and the right one.
